Maladaptive Strategies.value: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: The people responsible have faced no consequences
I am permanently an outsider now
I feel isolated and set apart from others

vignette: Samantha is a 35-year-old North American actress who has been experiencing significant distress following a traumatic event she witnessed at a local theater where she frequently performed. About six months ago, Samantha was at the theater for a rehearsal when she overheard an argument that escalated into a violent confrontation between two individuals outside the building. Despite her attempts to call for help and intervene, one of the individuals was violently attacked by the other in full view of Samantha and several audience members who were waiting to enter. Since that day, Samantha has been haunted by memories of the incident. When she thinks about it, it feels like she is reliving the event all over again, with a visceral sense of fear and horror washing over her. She describes these memories as fragmented pieces that don’t fit together coherently, making it difficult for her to put what happened into words. Samantha’s trauma has led her to adopt several maladaptive strategies to cope with her distress. One significant change is her avoidance of anything related to uniforms or weapons, particularly those associated with the military and police. This aversion extends even to public transportation, which she now avoids entirely due to the presence of uniformed personnel. Instead of taking buses or trains, Samantha relies on driving herself everywhere, which has increased her stress levels given her busy schedule. Her compulsive spending is another coping mechanism that has emerged post-trauma. She finds herself impulsively buying things to distract and comfort herself when she feels overwhelmed by negative emotions such as fear, anger, guilt, and shame. Despite knowing that these purchases are not sustainable financially, Samantha struggles to resist the urge to shop as a means of managing her intense feelings. Samantha has also developed a strong sense of safety-seeking behavior. She always chooses where to sit based on how safe or protected she feels in a given space. This includes selecting seats near exits during performances and meetings, which often leads to her feeling isolated from others because they don’t share the same need for proximity to escape routes. One of Samantha’s most significant struggles is trusting that she is truly safe even when others reassure her otherwise. Despite their reassurances, she finds it impossible to believe she is secure. This disbelief has led to increased anxiety in social settings and at work, where she feels constantly vigilant and on edge. The event has also reinforced a deep sense of isolation for Samantha. She believes that the people responsible have faced no consequences for their actions, which further solidifies her belief that she will always be an outsider looking in. This perception of being set apart from others has strained many of her relationships and has made it difficult for her to confide in friends or colleagues about what she is going through. Over time, Samantha’s avoidance behaviors have had tangible consequences on both her personal life and career. Her reluctance to use public transportation often causes her to arrive late to rehearsals and auditions, leading to missed opportunities and strained relationships with fellow actors and directors who depend on her punctuality. What finally brought Samantha to seek help was a culmination of these issues reaching a breaking point in her daily functioning. She is most afraid of becoming completely isolated and losing the career she loves due to her inability to manage her symptoms effectively. At the same time, she is hopeful that with professional support, she can regain some sense of control over her life and find ways to reintegrate into both her personal and professional worlds without feeling like an outsider or in constant danger. Through therapy, Samantha hopes to learn how to navigate her memories more effectively and begin to trust others again. She wants to break free from the patterns that have been holding her back and regain a sense of normalcy and safety in her daily life.
